note: Anonymized, per-speaker summaries of one workshop discussion. Participant labels follow the order of each speaker's first substantive contribution. Names, employers, organisations, camps, products, personal details and small talk were removed. There is deliberately no record of who is who.

voices.label: Participant A
voices.summary: Warns that misaligned incentives turn good technology harmful and that nobody consented to AI, and calls for interdisciplinary alignment work, modelling positive futures, and new economic and governance systems for human–AI co-evolution.
voices.content:
Gatherings like this shouldn't just pretend to discuss something important and then nothing happens. If we put this many smart people in a room, we should ask what tangible artifacts we can co-produce.

We can build incredible technology meant to do good, but when the incentives of the people building it are misaligned, it easily does more harm than good. Look at what happened with crypto: it started with inspiration and the promise of better financial systems, sovereignty and meritocracy, and the community ended up being leveraged for the profit of a few. But in that world people at least chose to participate and took on the financial risk knowingly. With AI there is no consent at all. None of us chose to participate or was even asked, and the consequences are far larger than losing money: it touches every area of our lives.

So human alignment matters as much as technical alignment. Even good technology can make things worse if the humans behind it are misaligned. We need interdisciplinary people in one room: neuroscience, evolutionary biology, cognitive science, plus contemplative practice and the traditions that have studied consciousness for thousands of years. We should model positive versions of the future and run experiments on how humans and AI can co-evolve, including what new economic and governance systems for human–AI coordination look like. Are we just going to let it develop on its own and let those who don't adapt fall away, or will we take agency and actively shape systems that serve humanity?

voices.label: Participant B
voices.summary: Sees AI as a tool whose goals humans must set rather than a decider of principles; puts consent and data capture first, especially artists' work used without permission; holds people responsible for robots and autonomous vehicles; and wants to start a messy shared draft now.
voices.content:
The big AI labs are focused on a drag race toward superintelligence and aren't really building for communities or people. I want to help change that.

One way real economic change happens is a coalition of companies that hold human-first principles foremost, enough of them that consumers have a real choice. The evidence is strong that this doesn't cost profits: companies with good governance that care about their users' communities actually do considerably better. The whole point of capitalism is choosing between products, and given an aligned choice I think people will pick it.

On using AI to write this: I agree with parts of what Participant E says, but AI is a tool, and the user decides what it's used for. It's wonderful math, but math with an optimization function that someone picked. I'm all for using it to find coherence between different perspectives, but we are the ones setting the goal and the style: how burners should use AI, and how AI can be used in line with the community's principles and ethos. What worries me is trusting the AI to adjudicate or decide what these principles should be.

The key chapters are consent, agency and accountability, and culture, and there will be areas we don't know yet. Today bringing a walking robot to the playa would be close to impossible; in five or ten years they could be walking among us, and today that isn't safe. A self-driving art car with nobody actually driving would be refused anywhere else. If you do it at all, it goes very slowly, someone is right next to it, and there are ways to shut it off. Rules about responsibility and accountability will largely rhyme with what the default world has already decided.

If I had to pick where to start, it's consent. People have very different views on data capture, and the community already has principles around photography and recording, so that's a reasonable foundation. Artists' concern that their work could be used as fodder for AI without their permission should be taken seriously.

On connectivity: before personal satellite internet, getting online out there was hard and unreliable. Now it's easy, and it has really helped coordination with the artists and camps we collaborate with. My camp has a culture of not being on our phones when we're together, but the rise of posting for social media over the last five years is definitely visible.

I'd also like to hear more voices; a small set of people has done most of the talking. And I'm curious what happens if we just get started: make ourselves all editors on a shared doc, write something, let it get ugly, then clean it up.

voices.label: Participant C
voices.summary: Supports AI for processing archives but insists that gathering and witnessing people's lived perspectives must stay a human process, even if it takes a year; frames this as a vision-coherence problem, not a technology problem, and sees no-money as a mechanism for decommodification.
voices.content:
AI gives us a way to close the narrative gap. There isn't a desire gap or even a value gap: the problem has been showing that human meaning and sustenance are compatible with a regenerative biosphere. The tools we've had, spreadsheets and investment returns that look at everything through compounding math, created a legibility crisis that leads to runaway destruction. AI can give people easy, accessible narrative tools to see what we're doing and what we were missing.

There is wisdom in the request that this be a human process. Of course we'll use spell check, email and all sorts of mechanistic tools, and using an LLM to process archival data is great. But when I sit on the playa and listen to someone, I take in their whole person. That kind of witnessing, holding space for pain, grief and joy, is not something LLMs are good at; they emit tokens as if they could, but I'm not convinced there's any interiority behind it. If an authentic constitution from the playa takes a year, we should say so. A slapdash job with an LLM and a web form is possible, but a heartfelt witnessing of what tens of thousands of people want, including people who hate AI, people who want to lean in, and artists who don't want their work taken in by anything, needs intentionality. That's something we should not abdicate.

I agree with Participant E that we shouldn't over-read the request: whatever we do, we shouldn't cheat and one-shot it. The question is what we are optimising for. Each of us calling ten burner friends is a pain, like walking barefoot to the Man, but some people do it, and there is value in the process. Use all the tools, with intention.

For next steps I'm the one who thinks we should start with a shared doc. We don't have a technology problem; we have a vision-coherence, zero-to-one problem. It will be a democracy of feet: the people who show up and do the work will shape it, and we need a rapid-prototyping, ship-it mentality. I love the idea of everyone drafting separately and then cross-editing.

On money: include it if it matters to you, but think about the difference between the mechanism and what it's meant to achieve. Having no money on the playa is a radical way to separate it from the default world and to force us to think about decommodification.

voices.label: Participant D
voices.summary: Frames the work as what AI can learn from Burning Man and vice versa, proposes chapters on consent and recording, agent accountability, and AI in culture and art, wants to test a one-shot AI draft against the human process, and insists the result keep mischief and fun.
voices.content:
A good way to frame this: what can AI learn from Burning Man, and what can Burning Man learn from AI? The constitution is a foundational document, inspired by the constitutions some AI labs have published for their models. We need to work out the trade-offs and negotiations that let us put our best foot forward on the ethical quandaries coming at us, and it could become a foundation for building or training models.

I first imagined thought leaders drafting it together, founding-fathers style. Participant E pointed out that the original principles came bottom-up, out of the camps. I think the smartest approach is to do both and see whether they converge on the same point. The project sponsor said it should be human-written; that didn't mean "don't use AI", it meant don't just prompt it and hand it over.

The areas I see so far: consent, recording and data capture; agents, agency and accountability (companies are responsible for their agents, and that should be in the constitution); and AI in culture, art and city life, such as AI-created art and camp operations. Do connectivity and phone culture belong in it too?

We can probably one-shot a pretty good "burner AI constitution" with today's tools. We should actually test that against the human process and compare; that comparison would be an interesting artifact in itself.

On recording, my starting point is: always assume you're being recorded. If you see someone recording you and you don't want that, there's a transaction: go up to them and ask them to please not record you. With camera glasses and similar devices there are edge cases all the time.

Research shows brainstorming separately and then merging beats sharing first, so everyone should write down their own thoughts, especially incidents they've personally encountered, before we merge. And while all this is serious and deep, don't forget the mischief and the fun. Any model we train or grow has to have that mischievous element too.

voices.label: Participant E
voices.summary: Argues it is hubris for humans to dictate how a future super-AI should think, and that refusing AI is irresponsible: everyone should write their own version, AI should find coherence across them and the culture's whole archive, and humans then make the final edit.
voices.content:
If this constitution is meant to inform how a model behaves, I think it's a bit of hubris to say we have the wisdom to tell a future super-AI how it should think. I'd rather create a process where it learns from a comprehensive understanding of the world: how this culture was created and lived over 40 years, related philosophies, and the inputs of everyone who wants to take part. The power of AI is taking unorganised, disparate data from many sources and finding the coherence inside it. Let's use that strength.

I'm not saying whatever it comes out with is gospel. It's an amazing tool for finding truth in disorganised data, integrating 20 people plus the thousands who have lived this culture, which no single person could do. Then we, as sovereign human agents, do the final editing and make the decisions.

Today, not using AI is actually irresponsible. We're not kids cheating on homework; this isn't a standard problem set. Getting 20 or 30 people to agree on one thing is very hard, especially remotely and piecemeal. Let the technology help.

I'm also not saying one-shot it. Everybody writes their own constitution, what they think it means. We add the archives: articles, poetry, films, documentaries and the other artifacts of 40 years. Then the prompt isn't "write me the constitution"; it's "here is each person's idea: where are we similar, where are we different, and how do we express that coherently?" That's very close to what Participant F describes. None of us is a founding father, so if you want buy-in, give people a chance to participate. This lets anyone who wants to participate do so.

I wouldn't take the sponsor's request too literally. My read is: don't take the shortcut, go through a rigorous process. Much of the material is public; a few searches produce a thousand links. Internal communications would take more effort. Even a rich group like ours is 17 people, and the community is millions over the years, so none of us can claim to represent all of those experiences.

voices.label: Participant F
voices.summary: Advocates a human-first process: write our own ideas first and ask AI for feedback afterwards, because AI-first drafting misses things and produces less original perspectives.
voices.content: There's a real difference between writing something yourself and then getting feedback from AI, versus asking AI to do it first and reacting to that. AI-first sometimes misses things, though it can also add things we don't see. Doing it human-first lets the work really come from us: these are our ideas and our creativity, and then we refer to the AI afterwards for feedback. In my experience you get a more interesting, innovative and unique perspective when you start human-first.

voices.label: Participant G
voices.summary: Says community buy-in matters more than a polished final draft, and proposes starting with a short, handwritten first version: messy, fast and human, without weeks of debate over AI tools.
voices.content:
Whoever writes the final document, we need buy-in, and that matters more than the final draft right now. I like the idea of a handwritten first version, literally pen to paper. It might be three lines long, but that's what gets buy-in from the community. If something handwritten came across my feed, whether one line or a whole manifesto, that's a much stronger pull than chasing perfection over whether the punctuation or a word is right. Don't let perfection be the enemy of progress. It should be messy, it should be fast, and it should be human. Then everyone knows we're building on something real, and the momentum grows. Find the lowest-hanging fruit before we end up in a three-week debate about which AI tool writes the whole thing.

For scale, there are debate-and-voting platforms built for thousands of people to deliberate and decide, but that's for thousands, not for 15 of us. Later, when it's time to ratify, we could invite the whole community into an immersive shared space. Teams that already film people on the playa with 360 cameras have learned a lot about how to do that, which overlaps with the recording questions.

voices.label: Participant H
voices.summary: Proposes drafting separately, cross-editing, then letting AI collate; asks whether AI's own views should be invited and whether money is in scope; and prefers a light-touch constitution, treating phone and social-media habits as culture rather than rules.
voices.content:
On the process: the proposal was that we each write a wish list for the constitution and then have AI help us analyse how our opinions relate to one another. Beyond that, to what extent should we ask AI for its own input, its own thoughts or conclusions, and not just a summary of what we said?

We should be nimble; with AI we just got started and look where we are. Have everyone interested write a first draft or key points, spend a couple of days cross-editing each other's work and leaving comments, then have AI compile and collate it all. In the meantime, rather than posting opinions and cross-pollinating before everyone has had a chance to think, share prompts and questions for others to noodle on.

A lot of my thinking is about financial laws for machines. We have them for humans and for nations. There's no money on the playa, but finances are a huge part of putting the event together, so should that be in scope here? AI's biggest problem is making itself sustainable, financially and environmentally, and the environmental side eventually drives the economic outcome.

On connectivity: before personal satellite internet I would probably have signed a petition against it. Now that it's here, communication and execution are much easier, much more gets done in the few days we have to build, and that makes everything more fun. Would I like to see less social-media posting at the event? Yes, but that's culture for experienced burners to pass down; it can't be written into laws. Like most governing documents, I prefer a lighter touch to a broad one. We don't need to dictate every single thing: if people don't want to use their phones, they shouldn't; if some do, they should be able to.

voices.label: Participant I
voices.summary: Asks what AI should not do: which precious parts of the experience, such as creative expression and how people connect, the constitution must protect from AI encroachment, and how connectivity has already changed them.
voices.content:
Besides what AI should do, we need to ask what it shouldn't do, and what we are trying to protect. Which aspects of the experience are precious or particularly valuable to us in a way we wouldn't want AI to encroach on? Is it creative expression? Is it how we connect? Which lived experiences are we trying to protect, and which are we trying to enable, that AI could encroach on?

This should be a key part of the constitution: which aspects of the culture and the experience do we want to protect, or support, with AI, and how do we protect their authenticity? I'd also like to hear from people who were there before and after personal satellite internet arrived: how did the experience change?

voices.label: Participant J
voices.summary: Wants a constitution that survives the test of time, written for AI broadly and for future eras of intelligence, consciousness and flourishing, not only for today's LLMs.
voices.content:
Burning Man has been a source of inspiration for wave after wave of technology coming out of the region. As we enter a new era of higher intelligence, consciousness and flourishing, closer to nature and closer to humanity, the constitution should be written across time, not fixed on this moment. Right now we focus on LLMs, but AI came through big data and many kinds of neural networks before that, and it will keep evolving. I want to make something that can survive the test of time, broader in scope in terms of both history and what's coming.

For tooling, a simple AI notebook tool would do: gather all the documents in one folder and generate idea maps, videos and decks from them easily.

voices.label: Participant K
voices.summary: Proposes using AI to build a framework of topics, letting everyone weigh in on the ones they care about, having AI report what has broad consensus, and taking only the real disagreements to live discussion.
voices.content:
I'm largely on the same page as Participant E. What we're struggling with is how to get a framework, maybe top-line bullet points, and then get everybody's opinion in. I'd use AI to create that framework of things we care about. Say it comes up with 30; we decide 10 aren't relevant and focus on 20. Then we find a way to give everybody a voice: all of us, plus whoever isn't in the room, can pick the topics that matter to them and add their opinions.

At the end it tells us, for example, that 30 people submitted opinions on data privacy, recording, or feeding art into building a robot, and what we agree on. For instance, there might be 80% consensus that we shouldn't photograph the temple so someone can build a robot replica of it. It also shows where there's only 20% agreement or a lot of disagreement. We put what we agree on in writing straight away, and take the disagreements to a separate live discussion with the people who are most invested in them. This would be fairly easy to build with an AI assistant.

I'll also separate my own areas of expertise from areas I'm curious about but don't know well, and bring those open questions to the next session for discussion.

voices.label: Participant L
voices.summary: Argues money is absolutely in scope, since staying solvent year-round is one of the event's biggest challenges and attending costs money; treats money as just another art supply and says decommodification must be decoupled from money itself.
voices.content: Money is absolutely relevant. It's one of the biggest problems the event has: how to stay solvent year-round. It also costs money to go. I've always looked at money as just an art supply, another medium. So the decommodification idea needs to be decoupled from money itself.

voices.label: Participant M
voices.summary: Offers to feed the event's history and publications into a model for an objective historical analysis, while also capturing people's subjective experiences: garbage in, garbage out, but genius in, genius out.
voices.content:
I've started gathering a timeline of the event's origins and some of its publications, and I'm happy to feed all of that into a model to see what it says about the history and culture: a more objective historical analysis to bring back to the group. But the culture of the event is so incredible that we should parse not only the objective arc of its history but also what people subjectively experience there. There are only a couple of dozen of us here, but we can pull from people's experiences and feed those in too.

We don't have a technology or model problem. Garbage in, garbage out, but also goodness in, goodness out, and genius in, genius out. There is so much genius in the community, the city and its history that once we start feeding it in and prompting, we'll get some really good results.

voices.label: Participant N
voices.summary: Describes the integration barrier between playa inspiration and the default world, where a gifting society depends on huge resources, and dreams of a less ephemeral, year-round counterpart where discoveries could take root.
voices.content:
There is so much brilliance on the playa during our stay. It's eye-opening: you see all the different ways society could be, and you want to bring that back to the default world, because life on earth could be so much kinder and more benevolent to the people living here. That inspiration is super valuable.

But there's an integration barrier. You come back and have to face the fact that it takes a huge influx of resources and capital to create the context, in a harsh place, that props up our gifting society and its karmic economy. You can create little pockets that differ enough from default capitalism to integrate some of what we discover in that vast prototyping ground, but I've always wanted a counterpart with facets that are less ephemeral. If something were built to stay year-round, it would create a different context for integrating what we learn afterwards.
